disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce distress or prevent a feared event), which are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and the course is usually chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress; many patients have partial insight, recognizing their thoughts and behaviors as excessive. OCD is distinguished from anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder by the ego-dystonic, intrusive quality of the thoughts and the ritualistic, often clearly irrational behaviors aimed at neutralizing them. It can be exacerbated by life stressors, high-responsibility roles, or environments that reward perfectionism and hypervigilance, and is frequently comorbid with depression and other anxiety disorders.

narrative.personality: James is an outgoing, imaginative, and data-driven problem-solver who thrives on creative collaboration and late-night artistic projects but tends to overthink and procrastinate under pressure.
narrative.stressor: James traces the beginning of his difficulties to about a year after he transitioned from an internal engineering support role into a high-stakes client-facing sales engineer position, where he suddenly became personally responsible for large contracts and complex technical guarantees. The combination of aggressive quarterly targets, frequent travel, and the expectation that he flawlessly anticipate every possible failure scenario led him to spend longer and longer hours poring over specs and emails, replaying conversations and second-guessing whether he might have missed some critical detail. Over time, what started as conscientiousness morphed into rigid, time-consuming internal checking routines before presentations and after client calls, eating into his sleep and pushing his nightly sketching from a source of relaxation into yet another arena where he felt he could make catastrophic mistakes. He finally sought psychiatric care after his manager noted his growing delays in turning around proposals, his girlfriend commented that he seemed mentally “elsewhere” even during social events, and he realized he was losing billable time and creative work hours to repetitive mental review he couldn’t easily shut off.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting these unwanted thoughts stuck in my head about things going wrong at work, and no matter how much I try to push them away, they just keep coming back and taking over my day.”

narrative.personality: Patricia is meticulous, hyper-organized, and observant, balancing a disciplined, safety-focused mindset with a reflective, artistic side and a strong sense of responsibility toward others.
narrative.stressor: Patricia’s problems intensified after she was promoted to a de facto lead role on the night shift in the casino surveillance room, following an incident in which a colleague missed a cheating scheme and the entire team was reprimanded. Already proud of her ability to catch tiny irregularities on CCTV, she began to feel personally accountable for preventing every possible theft, altercation, or self-harm event on the floor, especially during understaffed overnight shifts when she knew fewer eyes were on the monitors. Gradually, her work habits shifted from careful monitoring to elaborate, rigid routines of re-watching footage and double- or triple-documenting minor events before she could allow herself to move on, routines that spilled over into her home life as she created similar repetitive rituals around locks, appliances, and even her art supplies. She sought psychiatric help only after her exhaustion and lateness from extended end-of-shift “just one more check” cycles put her promotion at risk and her spouse expressed alarm that their evenings had become dominated by her need to repeatedly perform specific actions before she could sit down or go to bed.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I have to keep doing the same things over and over, at work and at home, or I get so anxious that I can’t relax or move on.”

narrative.personality: Dieu is a highly curious, methodical, and competitive young adult who likes structure and self-improvement, balancing social engagement with solitary creative and intellectual pursuits.
narrative.stressor: Dieu first noticed changes after moving out of his parents’ home and starting his full-time customer service job, a transition that combined new financial responsibilities, performance metrics, and the pressure of being the first in his family to secure an office-based role. Initially, his natural organization helped him excel, but as call volumes and targets ramped up, he became preoccupied with the possibility of making errors that might affect customers or jeopardize his goal of quickly advancing to a team lead position. What began as double-checking tickets and scripts slowly evolved into elaborate routines around how he reviewed cases, documented interactions, and prepared his workstation, which he felt compelled to complete before he could start or end a shift, and similar patterns emerged at home around cooking, journaling, and gaming. He decided to seek psychiatric evaluation when these routines started making him late to work, crowding out his social plans and badminton practice, and leaving him feeling trapped by habits he intellectually recognized as excessive but could not easily cut back.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve gotten stuck doing these repetitive little routines to feel okay before I can start or finish things, and they’re starting to slow me down at work and in my daily life.”
